Sound: S1 “lub”
Definition (whole): First heart sound = closure of the AV valves (mitral M1 → tricuspid T1) at the start of ventricular systole.
Word-by-word: S = sound · 1 = first in the cycle · M1 = mitral, T1 = tricuspid component.
When / phase heard: Start of systole (isovolumetric contraction). Just after QRS; with carotid upstroke.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Ventricle depolarizes (QRS) → contracts 2 LV pressure rises > LA pressure 3 Mitral (then tricuspid) leaflets snap shut 4 Sudden deceleration of blood → vibration of valves/walls = S1
Inspiration vs expiration: Little change. M1–T1 split (rarely heard, LLSB) may widen slightly on inspiration.
Diseases / conditions: Loud: short PR, early MS, tachycardia/hyperdynamic (fever, anemia, thyrotoxicosis). Soft: long PR (1° AV block), MR, calcified MS, LV failure, obesity/COPD/effusion. Variable: AF, complete heart block.
Where & how to listen: Apex (M1), LLSB (T1). Diaphragm.
Key pearl: Loudest at apex (S1 > S2 there). Time it with the carotid pulse to identify systole.

Sound: S2 “dub”
Definition (whole): Second heart sound = closure of the semilunar valves (aortic A2 → pulmonic P2) at the end of systole.
Word-by-word: S = sound · 2 = second · A2 = aortic, P2 = pulmonic closure.
When / phase heard: End of systole / start of diastole (isovolumetric relaxation). ~ end of T wave.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Ejection ends; ventricles relax 2 Ventricular pressure falls < aortic & pulmonary artery pressure 3 Backflow snaps aortic cusps shut (A2), then pulmonic (P2) 4 P2 later: low-resistance, compliant pulmonary bed → longer ‘hangout interval’
Inspiration vs expiration: Normally splits on inspiration, single on expiration (see C).
Diseases / conditions: Normal. Abnormal forms → C & D. Single S2: elderly (P2 inaudible), severe AS, pulmonary atresia, TGA, truncus, emphysema.
Where & how to listen: Base: 2nd RICS (A2), 2nd–3rd LICS (P2 & split). Diaphragm.
Key pearl: A2 is normally louder everywhere; P2 heard only at pulmonic area. S2 > S1 at the base.

Sound: S3 “ventricular gallop”
Definition (whole): Low-pitched early-diastolic sound from rapid passive filling of a volume-loaded/dilated ventricle.
Word-by-word: S3 = third sound · Ventricular = arises in ventricle · Protodiastolic = early (proto) diastole.
When / phase heard: Early diastole, 0.12–0.18 s after S2 — rapid ventricular filling phase.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 AV valve opens → atrial blood rushes into ventricle 2 High volume/flow or dilated, poorly compliant ventricle 3 Ventricle reaches its elastic limit → inflow decelerates abruptly (chordae tense) 4 Vibration of ventricular wall = S3
Inspiration vs expiration: LV S3 ↑ on expiration; RV S3 ↑ on inspiration.
Diseases / conditions: Physiologic (<40 y): children, athletes, pregnancy, high output. Pathologic: HFrEF, dilated CMP, severe MR/TR, AR, large VSD/PDA, thyrotoxicosis, anemia.
Where & how to listen: Bell, light pressure, apex, left lateral decubitus, end-expiration. RV: LLSB.
Key pearl: Cadence “Ken-tuc-KY” (S1-S2-S3). Pathologic after 40. Absent in severe MS (inflow blocked).

Sound: S4 “atrial gallop”
Definition (whole): Low-pitched late-diastolic sound from atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle.
Word-by-word: S4 = fourth sound · Atrial = caused by atrial kick · Presystolic = just before systole.
When / phase heard: Late diastole, just before S1 (after P wave) — atrial systole phase.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Hypertrophied/ischemic ventricle → ↓ compliance 2 Atrium contracts forcefully (atrial kick) to fill it 3 Blood meets non-compliant wall → abrupt wall tensing 4 Vibration = S4 (needs atrial contraction!)
Inspiration vs expiration: LV S4 ↑ on expiration; RV S4 ↑ on inspiration.
Diseases / conditions: HTN heart disease/LVH, aortic stenosis, HCM, acute MI/ ischemia, restrictive CMP, elderly. RV: pulmonary HTN, PS.
Where & how to listen: Bell, apex, left lateral decubitus. RV: LLSB.
Key pearl: Cadence “TEN-nes-see” (S4-S1-S2). Almost always pathologic. Never in AF (no atrial kick).

Sound: S3 gallop
Definition (whole): Triple rhythm S1-S2-S3 at a fast rate resembling a galloping horse = pathologic S3.
Word-by-word: Gallop = 3-beat cadence of a horse · S3 = the added early-diastolic beat.
When / phase heard: Early diastole (rapid filling).
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Failing LV → ↑ end-systolic volume & filling pressure 2 ↑ LA pressure → forceful early inflow into dilated LV 3 Abrupt deceleration → loud S3 4 Compensatory tachycardia → galloping cadence
Inspiration vs expiration: LV: louder on expiration.
Diseases / conditions: Decompensated HFrEF, dilated CMP, acute MI with LV failure, severe MR, high-output HF.
Where & how to listen: Bell, apex, LLD.
Key pearl: Sign of ↑ filling pressure; poor prognosis; fades with diuresis.

Sound: S4 gallop
Definition (whole): Triple rhythm S4-S1-S2 at a fast rate = pathologic S4.
Word-by-word: Gallop + S4 = the added presystolic beat.
When / phase heard: Late diastole (atrial systole).
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Stiff/hypertrophied or ischemic LV 2 Strong atrial kick against high LVEDP 3 Abrupt wall tensing → loud S4 4 Tachycardia → gallop cadence
Inspiration vs expiration: LV: louder on expiration.
Diseases / conditions: HTN crisis/LVH, AS, HCM, acute ischemia (during angina/MI), restrictive CMP.
Where & how to listen: Bell, apex, LLD.
Key pearl: Diastolic (relaxation) dysfunction marker. Absent in AF.

Sound: Summation gallop
Definition (whole): S3 + S4 fuse into one loud mid-diastolic sound when HR is fast (>~120).
Word-by-word: Summation = adding together. (At slower HR both = quadruple rhythm.)
When / phase heard: Mid-diastole.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Tachycardia shortens diastole 2 Rapid-filling & atrial-kick phases overlap 3 S3 + S4 superimpose → one loud sound
Inspiration vs expiration: LV: louder on expiration.
Diseases / conditions: Advanced HF with tachycardia.
Where & how to listen: Bell, apex.
Key pearl: Slow the HR (e.g., carotid massage) → may separate into S3 & S4.

Sound: Split S2 (general)
Definition (whole): Audible separation of S2 into A2 and P2.
Word-by-word: Split = divided in two · S2 = second sound.
When / phase heard: S2. Normal gap <30 ms (exp) → 40–80 ms (insp).
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Anything that delays P2 (long RV ejection, RBBB, ↑ pulm. capacitance) or advances A2 (short LV ejection) → wider split 2 Anything that delays A2 → narrow/reversed split
Inspiration vs expiration: Depends on type (below).
Diseases / conditions: Normal · wide · fixed · paradoxical · single.
Where & how to listen: 2nd–3rd LICS, diaphragm, supine (sitting may abolish physiologic split).
Key pearl: Always ask 2 questions: Is it split on expiration? Does it change with breathing?

Sound: Physiologic split
Definition (whole): Normal split that appears on inspiration and disappears on expiration.
Word-by-word: Physiologic = normal body function (not disease).
When / phase heard: S2 during inspiration.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Inspiration → ↓ intrathoracic pressure 2 ↑ venous return to RA/RV → ↑ RV stroke volume → longer RV ejection → P2 later 3 ↑ pulmonary capacitance (longer hangout) → P2 later 4 Blood pools in lungs → ↓ LV return → shorter LV ejection → A2 earlier 5 Expiration reverses → single S2
Inspiration vs expiration: Insp: split · Exp: single.
Diseases / conditions: Normal — esp. children & young adults.
Where & how to listen: Pulmonic area, supine.
Key pearl: Most obvious in the young; often inaudible in elderly.

Sound: Wide split
Definition (whole): Split heard on both phases, widening further on inspiration (respiratory variation preserved).
Word-by-word: Wide = gap larger than normal.
When / phase heard: S2, both phases.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Delayed P2: RBBB (late RV activation), pulmonic stenosis/PHT/PE (prolonged RV ejection) 2 Early A2: MR, VSD (LV empties by a second outlet → short LV ejection) 3 Normal respiratory effect still added on top
Inspiration vs expiration: Insp: wider · Exp: still split.
Diseases / conditions: RBBB, pulmonic stenosis, acute PE, pulmonary HTN with RV failure, MR, VSD, WPW (LV pre-excitation).
Where & how to listen: Pulmonic area.
Key pearl: Key difference from fixed split: it still varies with breathing.

Sound: Fixed split = Wide fixed split
Definition (whole): Wide split that does not change with respiration.
Word-by-word: Fixed = constant gap · Wide = larger than normal (fixed split is always wide).
When / phase heard: S2, both phases (same width).
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 ASD: L→R shunt at atrial level → chronic RV volume overload → long RV ejection → late P2 (wide) 2 Insp: ↑ systemic return to RA but ↑ RA pressure → ↓ L→R shunt 3 Exp: ↓ systemic return but ↑ L→R shunt 4 Total RV filling stays ~constant (atria share pressure) → gap fixed
Inspiration vs expiration: Insp = Exp (no change).
Diseases / conditions: ASD (secundum = classic), partial anomalous pulmonary venous return, severe RV failure.
Where & how to listen: Pulmonic area.
Key pearl: ASD also: pulmonic flow ejection murmur (LUSB) ± tricuspid flow rumble — murmur is not from the hole.

Sound: Paradoxical split = Reversed split
Definition (whole): A2 delayed after P2: split heard on expiration, disappears on inspiration.
Word-by-word: Paradoxical = opposite of expected · Reversed = order becomes P2 → A2.
When / phase heard: S2 during expiration.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Delayed LV activation or prolonged LV ejection → A2 after P2 2 Insp: P2 moves later → toward A2 → single 3 Exp: P2 moves earlier → away from A2 → split
Inspiration vs expiration: Insp: single · Exp: split.
Diseases / conditions: LBBB (most common), RV pacing, severe AS, HOCM, severe HTN, acute ischemia/LV failure, large PDA, WPW (RV pre- excitation).
Where & how to listen: Pulmonic area.
Key pearl: Think “left side is late”: LBBB, AS, LV failure.

Sound: Single S2
Definition (whole): Only one S2 component is heard on both inspiration and expiration (no audible split).
Word-by-word: Single = one · S2 = second sound (A2 & P2 fused, or one of them absent).
When / phase heard: S2, both phases.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 A2 absent: calcified, immobile aortic valve (severe AS) 2 P2 inaudible/absent: elderly, emphysema/obesity, pulmonary atresia, TOF (tiny stenotic P valve), TGA (P valve posterior, aorta anterior) 3 Only one semilunar valve: truncus arteriosus 4 A2 & P2 coincide: severe PHT/Eisenmenger (narrow split), paradoxical split during inspiration
Inspiration vs expiration: Insp = Exp (single in both).
Diseases / conditions: Elderly (normal), emphysema, severe AS, pulmonary atresia, Tetralogy of Fallot, truncus arteriosus, TGA, Eisenmenger/ severe PHT.
Where & how to listen: Pulmonic area, diaphragm, supine.
Key pearl: Older adult: usually benign (P2 too soft). Cyanotic newborn + single S2 → think TOF, truncus, TGA.

Sound: Loud P2
Definition (whole): Accentuated pulmonic component of S2 (P2 ≥ A2 at pulmonic area, or P2 heard at the apex).
Word-by-word: Loud = ↑ intensity · P2 = pulmonic valve closure.
When / phase heard: S2, after A2 (end of RV systole).
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 ↑ Pulmonary artery pressure 2 ↑ Diastolic pressure gradient across pulmonic valve 3 Cusps slam shut more forcefully → loud P2
Inspiration vs expiration: Louder & more separated on inspiration.
Diseases / conditions: Pulmonary HTN: PAH, COPD/ILD (cor pulmonale), chronic/ acute PE, left HF, mitral stenosis, L→R shunts/Eisenmenger, OSA, altitude.
Where & how to listen: 2nd LICS (and apex), diaphragm.
Key pearl: May be palpable + RV heave. Normally louder in children/thin chests.

Sound: Loud A2
Definition (whole): Accentuated aortic component of S2.
Word-by-word: Loud = ↑ intensity · A2 = aortic valve closure.
When / phase heard: S2 (first component).
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 ↑ Aortic diastolic pressure (HTN) → stronger closing force 2 Or dilated aortic root sits closer to chest wall → ‘ringing/tambour’ A2
Inspiration vs expiration: Little change (both phases).
Diseases / conditions: Systemic HTN, aortic root dilation (Marfan, aortitis/syphilis, aneurysm), coarctation, TGA (anterior aorta). Soft A2: calcified AS, AR.
Where & how to listen: 2nd RICS, diaphragm.
Key pearl: Soft/absent A2 + ejection murmur = severe (calcified) AS.

boxes.x:
Sound: Opening snap (OS)
Definition (whole): High-pitched early-diastolic sound from a stenotic mitral valve snapping open.
Word-by-word: Opening = valve opening · Snap = sharp, crisp.
When / phase heard: Early diastole, 0.04–0.12 s after A2 (earlier than S3).
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Rheumatic commissural fusion → ↑ LA pressure 2 When LV pressure < LA, domed leaflets open 3 Abrupt tensing of stiff leaflets → snap 4 Followed by diastolic rumble
Inspiration vs expiration: Little change.
Diseases / conditions: Mitral stenosis (rheumatic); rarely tricuspid stenosis.
Where & how to listen: Apex–LLSB, diaphragm.
Key pearl: Shorter A2–OS = more severe MS. Lost when valve heavily calcified.

Sound: Ejection click
Definition (whole): High-pitched early-systolic sound just after S1.
Word-by-word: Ejection = at onset of ejection · Click = short, sharp.
When / phase heard: Early systole.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Stenotic-but-mobile semilunar valve (or dilated root) 2 Leaflets dome abruptly at opening → click
Inspiration vs expiration: Aortic: no change. Pulmonic: softer on inspiration (only right-sided exception).
Diseases / conditions: Bicuspid aortic valve, congenital AS, pulmonic stenosis, PHT, dilated aorta.
Where & how to listen: Aortic: apex/base. Pulmonic: LUSB.
Key pearl: Disappears as the valve calcifies (immobile).

Sound: Mid-systolic click
Definition (whole): Mid–late systolic click of mitral valve prolapse.
Word-by-word: Mid-systolic = middle of systole.
When / phase heard: Mid systole.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Redundant leaflet prolapses into LA 2 Chordae/leaflet suddenly tense → click ± late systolic murmur
Inspiration vs expiration: No significant change.
Diseases / conditions: MVP (myxomatous; Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos).
Where & how to listen: Apex, diaphragm.
Key pearl: ↓ LV volume (standing, Valsalva) → earlier click; squat/handgrip → later.

Sound: Pericardial knock / Tumor plop
Definition (whole): Knock: high-pitched early-diastolic sound in constrictive pericarditis. Plop: atrial myxoma prolapsing into ventricle.
Word-by-word: Knock = abrupt stop · Plop = tumor dropping.
When / phase heard: Early diastole (knock earlier than S3).
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Knock: rigid pericardium abruptly halts early filling 2 Plop: pedunculated tumor falls through AV valve and stops
Inspiration vs expiration: Knock: ↑ with inspiration. Plop: varies with position.
Diseases / conditions: Constrictive pericarditis (TB, post-surgery, radiation) · left atrial myxoma.
Where & how to listen: LLSB/apex, diaphragm.
Key pearl: Knock + Kussmaul sign. Plop + positional murmur, syncope, emboli.

boxes.x:
Respiration rule (Carvallo)
Inspiration ↑ venous return to right heart → right-sided sounds/
murmurs louder. Expiration → left-sided louder. Exception: pulmonic
ejection click softer on inspiration.

Bell vs diaphragm
Bell (light touch) = low pitch: S3, S4, MS rumble. Diaphragm (firm) =
high pitch: S1, S2, splits, clicks, OS, knock, AR. Firm bell pressure
makes S3/S4 fade.

Early-diastolic sound after S2?
Split S2 (≤0.06 s, base, both high) → OS (0.04–0.12 s, high, MS) →
Knock (0.10–0.12 s, high) → S3 (0.12–0.18 s, low, apex, bell).

Sound before S1?
S4 = low pitch, apex, bell, gone in AF. Split S1 = both high pitch,
LLSB, diaphragm. Ejection click = after S1, high pitch.

Auscultation areas
Aortic 2nd RICS · Pulmonic 2nd LICS · Erb's 3rd LICS · Tricuspid 4th
LICS/LLSB · Mitral apex 5th ICS MCL (“All Physicians Take Money”).

Murmur: Aortic stenosis AS
Definition (whole): Harsh crescendo–decrescendo systolic ejection murmur from flow through a narrowed aortic valve.
Word-by-word: Aortic = aortic valve · Stenosis (Gk stenos) = narrowing.
When / phase heard: Midsystole (ejection): starts after S1 (± ejection click), ends before A2.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Calcification/fusion → ↓ valve area 2 LV must generate high pressure → LV–aortic gradient 3 High-velocity turbulent jet rises & falls with ejection → diamond murmur 4 Pressure overload → concentric LVH → S4; severe: late-peaking murmur, soft A2, paradoxical split
Inspiration, expiration & maneuvers: Louder on expiration. ↓ Valsalva/ standing/handgrip; ↑ squat/leg raise; ↑ beat after PVC.
Diseases / conditions: Senile calcific (>65), bicuspid valve (<65), rheumatic (with MS). Symptoms: Syncope, Angina, Dyspnea/HF.
Where & how to listen: 2nd RICS, diaphragm, sitting forward. Radiates to carotids.
Key pearl: Pulsus parvus et tardus. Later peak = more severe. Aortic sclerosis: same murmur, normal pulse & A2.

Murmur: Hypertrophic obstructive CMP HOCM
Definition (whole): Systolic ejection murmur from dynamic LV outflow obstruction by a thick septum ± SAM of mitral leaflet.
Word-by-word: Hypertrophic = thickened · Obstructive = blocks outflow · Cardio-myo-pathy = heart-muscle disease.
When / phase heard: Midsystole; often with late MR.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Sarcomere mutation → asymmetric septal hypertrophy 2 Narrow LVOT → fast flow drags anterior mitral leaflet forward (Venturi → SAM) 3 Dynamic obstruction + MR → murmur 4 Smaller LV cavity = more obstruction
Inspiration, expiration & maneuvers: Little resp change. ↑ Valsalva/standing; ↓ squat, handgrip, leg raise.
Diseases / conditions: Familial HCM (AD; β-MHC, MYBPC3); sudden death in young athletes.
Where & how to listen: LLSB/apex. No carotid radiation.
Key pearl: With MVP, the only murmur ↑ by Valsalva. S4, bisferiens pulse.

Murmur: Pulmonic stenosis PS
Definition (whole): Systolic ejection murmur from flow through a narrowed pulmonic valve.
Word-by-word: Pulmonic = pulmonary valve · Stenosis = narrowing.
When / phase heard: Midsystole, after an ejection click (valvular).
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Fused/dysplastic valve → RV–PA gradient 2 Turbulent jet → murmur 3 Prolonged RV ejection → late, soft P2 → wide split 4 RV pressure overload → RVH, RV heave
Inspiration, expiration & maneuvers: ↑ on inspiration (click ↓ on inspiration).
Diseases / conditions: Congenital, Noonan, Tetralogy of Fallot, congenital rubella, carcinoid.
Where & how to listen: 2nd LICS; radiates to left shoulder/ back.
Key pearl: Longer murmur + later P2 = more severe.

Murmur: Atrial septal defect ASD (flow murmur)
Definition (whole): Systolic ejection murmur from ↑ flow across a normal pulmonic valve due to atrial L→R shunt.
Word-by-word: Atrial Septal Defect = hole in the wall between the atria.
When / phase heard: Midsystole + wide fixed split S2 ± mid-diastolic tricuspid flow rumble.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 LA pressure > RA → L→R shunt 2 RV & pulmonary volume overload 3 ↑ flow across normal pulmonic valve (relative PS) → murmur 4 Flow across ASD itself: low gradient → silent
Inspiration, expiration & maneuvers: Split fixed; murmur mildly ↑ inspiration.
Diseases / conditions: Secundum (most), primum (Down syndrome), sinus venosus; paradoxical emboli; Eisenmenger.
Where & how to listen: 2nd–3rd LICS.
Key pearl: The hole is silent — the key sign is the fixed split.

boxes.t: Innocent / flow murmurs · Still's · pulmonary flow
boxes.x:
Murmur: Innocent / flow murmurs Still's · pulmonary flow
Definition (whole): Soft systolic ejection murmurs in a structurally normal heart.
Word-by-word: Innocent = harmless · Functional / flow = from ↑ flow, not disease.
When / phase heard: Early–midsystole, grade ≤2/6.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Normal or ↑ stroke volume (high-output state) 2 Fast flow through normal outflow tracts 3 Mild turbulence/vibration of normal structures
Inspiration, expiration & maneuvers: Changes with posture; louder supine, softer standing.
Diseases / conditions: Children (Still's = musical/vibratory, LLSB; pulmonary flow, LUSB), pregnancy, anemia, fever, thyrotoxicosis, athletes.
Where & how to listen: LLSB / LUSB.
Key pearl: 7 S: Soft, Systolic, Short, Single S2 normal, Small area, Sweet, Sensitive to position.

Murmur: Chronic mitral regurgitation MR
Definition (whole): Blowing holosystolic murmur from backflow LV → LA through an incompetent mitral valve.
Word-by-word: Mitral = bishop's-mitre valve · Regurgitation = backward flow.
When / phase heard: Holosystolic: begins with S1, extends to/through A2 (plateau).
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Leaflet/annulus/chordae/papillary dysfunction → poor coaptation 2 LV > LA pressure from S1 to S2 → leak all systole → plateau murmur 3 LA & LV volume overload → dilation → S3, AF 4 ↓ forward flow → HF
Inspiration, expiration & maneuvers: ↑ expiration. ↑ handgrip/squat (afterload); ↓ Valsalva, amyl nitrite.
Diseases / conditions: MVP, rheumatic, ischemic papillary dysfunction, dilated CMP (functional), endocarditis, HCM.
Where & how to listen: Apex → radiates to axilla; diaphragm, LLD.
Key pearl: Soft S1 + S3 = severe MR. Early A2 → wide split S2.

Murmur: Tricuspid regurgitation TR
Definition (whole): Holosystolic murmur from backflow RV → RA.
Word-by-word: Tricuspid = three-cusped right AV valve · Regurgitation.
When / phase heard: Holosystolic.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 RV dilation (mostly from PHT) → annulus stretches 2 Poor coaptation → RV → RA leak all systole 3 ↑ RA pressure → giant v (CV) waves, pulsatile liver, edema
Inspiration, expiration & maneuvers: ↑ on inspiration (Carvallo sign).
Diseases / conditions: Functional (PHT, left HF), IV-drug endocarditis, carcinoid, Ebstein anomaly, rheumatic, pacemaker lead.
Where & how to listen: LLSB, radiates to right sternal border.
Key pearl: Look at JVP (CV waves) & liver.

Murmur: Ventricular septal defect VSD
Definition (whole): Harsh holosystolic murmur from L→R shunt across the ventricular septum.
Word-by-word: Ventricular Septal Defect = hole in the wall between the ventricles.
When / phase heard: Holosystolic.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 LV ≫ RV pressure throughout systole 2 High-velocity jet through defect → harsh murmur + thrill 3 ↑ pulmonary flow → LA/LV overload (± mitral flow rumble) 4 Chronic → PHT → Eisenmenger: shunt reverses, murmur fades, cyanosis
Inspiration, expiration & maneuvers: Little change. ↑ handgrip.
Diseases / conditions: Most common congenital defect; Down syndrome, TOF, post- MI septal rupture (3–5 days).
Where & how to listen: LLSB (3rd–4th LICS); thrill.
Key pearl: Smaller hole = louder murmur.

Murmur: Mitral valve prolapse MVP
Definition (whole): Mid-systolic click followed by a late-systolic murmur.
Word-by-word: Prolapse = slipping forward/down (leaflet bulges into LA).
When / phase heard: Mid-to-late systole, after the click.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Myxomatous degeneration → redundant leaflets, long chordae 2 Mid-systole: leaflet billows into LA → chordae snap tight = click 3 Coaptation lost → late-systolic MR
Inspiration, expiration & maneuvers: No resp change. Valsalva/standing → earlier click, longer murmur; squat → later.
Diseases / conditions: Primary myxomatous, Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos, ADPKD.
Where & how to listen: Apex, diaphragm.
Key pearl: Most common valve lesion; may progress to MR/ chordal rupture.

Murmur: Acute mitral regurgitation
Definition (whole): Short, early-systolic decrescendo murmur of sudden severe MR into a small, stiff LA.
Word-by-word: Acute = sudden onset.
When / phase heard: Early systole, decrescendo.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Sudden papillary/chordal rupture or endocarditis 2 Large volume into normal-size LA → LA pressure rises fast 3 LV–LA gradient falls late in systole → murmur short/soft 4 Flash pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock
Inspiration, expiration & maneuvers: ↑ expiration.
Diseases / conditions: Post-MI papillary muscle rupture (inferior MI, posteromedial), endocarditis, chordal rupture.
Where & how to listen: Apex (may be soft/absent).
Key pearl: New murmur + sudden pulmonary edema after MI → urgent echo.

cols.h: D · EARLY-DIASTOLIC MURMURS (decrescendo, starts at S2)

boxes.x:
Murmur: Aortic regurgitation AR
Definition (whole): High-pitched, blowing early-diastolic decrescendo murmur from backflow aorta → LV.
Word-by-word: Aortic valve · Regurgitation = backward flow.
When / phase heard: Early diastole, starts right at A2, decrescendo.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Leaflet or aortic-root disease → incompetent valve 2 Aortic diastolic pressure > LV → backflow; gradient largest at start → decrescendo 3 LV volume overload → eccentric hypertrophy 4 ↑ stroke volume + ↓ diastolic BP → wide pulse pressure
Inspiration, expiration & maneuvers: ↑ expiration. ↑ handgrip; ↓ amyl nitrite.
Diseases / conditions: Bicuspid, rheumatic, endocarditis, root dilation (Marfan, HTN, syphilis, ankylosing spondylitis, dissection).
Where & how to listen: Erb's point/LSB (valve), RSB (root); sit up, lean forward, end-expiration, diaphragm.
Key pearl: Bounding pulse: Corrigan, de Musset, Quincke, Duroziez. Acute AR = short murmur.

Murmur: Pulmonic regurgitation PR · Graham Steell
Definition (whole): Early-diastolic decrescendo murmur from backflow PA → RV; Graham Steell = high-pitched PR from PHT.
Word-by-word: Pulmonic Regurgitation; Graham Steell = physician who described it (1888).
When / phase heard: Early diastole, after P2.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 PHT → dilated PA & annulus 2 Incompetent valve → high-pressure backflow 3 High-pitched murmur (low-pitched if PA pressure normal)
Inspiration, expiration & maneuvers: ↑ on inspiration.
Diseases / conditions: PHT (MS, COPD, PAH), post-TOF repair, endocarditis.
Where & how to listen: 2nd–3rd LICS.
Key pearl: Loud P2 + early diastolic murmur ↑ on inspiration = Graham Steell.

Murmur: Mitral stenosis MS
Definition (whole): Low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble with presystolic accentuation from flow through a narrowed mitral valve.
Word-by-word: Mitral valve · Stenosis = narrowing.
When / phase heard: Mid-diastole after opening snap; presystolic ↑ (atrial kick) — lost in AF.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Rheumatic commissural fusion → ↓ valve area 2 LA–LV diastolic gradient → turbulent inflow → rumble 3 ↑ LA pressure → LA enlargement (AF, thrombus, dysphagia, Ortner hoarseness) 4 Pulmonary venous HTN → PHT → loud P2, RV failure
Inspiration, expiration & maneuvers: ↑ expiration; ↑ after exercise, LLD.
Diseases / conditions: Rheumatic heart disease (most), mitral annular calcification; unmasked by pregnancy.
Where & how to listen: Apex, bell, LLD; very localized.
Key pearl: Loud S1 + OS + rumble. Shorter A2–OS / longer rumble = severe.

Murmur: Tricuspid stenosis TS
Definition (whole): Mid-diastolic rumble through a stenotic tricuspid valve.
Word-by-word: Tricuspid valve · Stenosis.
When / phase heard: Mid-diastole, presystolic ↑.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Leaflet fusion → RA–RV gradient → rumble 2 ↑ RA pressure → giant a waves, hepatomegaly, edema
Inspiration, expiration & maneuvers: ↑ on inspiration.
Diseases / conditions: Rheumatic (with MS), carcinoid.
Where & how to listen: LLSB, bell.
Key pearl: Giant a waves, slow y descent.

Murmur: Austin Flint murmur
Definition (whole): Apical mid-diastolic rumble in severe AR without organic MS.
Word-by-word: Austin Flint = US physician (1862).
When / phase heard: Mid/late diastole.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 AR jet hits anterior mitral leaflet → partially closes it (functional MS) 2 ↑ LV diastolic pressure 3 Turbulent mitral inflow → rumble
Inspiration, expiration & maneuvers: ↑ expiration; ↓ amyl nitrite (MS ↑).
Diseases / conditions: Severe chronic AR.
Where & how to listen: Apex, bell.
Key pearl: No opening snap, no loud S1 (vs true MS).

Murmur: Carey Coombs murmur
Definition (whole): Soft apical mid-diastolic murmur in acute rheumatic fever.
Word-by-word: Carey Coombs = British physician (1924).
When / phase heard: Mid-diastole.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Acute rheumatic carditis → mitral valvulitis 2 Edematous, inflamed leaflets → turbulent inflow → soft rumble
Inspiration, expiration & maneuvers: ↑ expiration.
Diseases / conditions: Acute rheumatic fever (carditis).
Where & how to listen: Apex, bell.
Key pearl: Transient; no OS; fades with recovery.

boxes.t: Diastolic flow rumbles · relative MS / TS
boxes.x:
Murmur: Diastolic flow rumbles relative MS / TS
Definition (whole): Mid-diastolic rumble from ↑ flow across a normal AV valve.
Word-by-word: Relative / functional stenosis = valve normal, flow too large.
When / phase heard: Mid-diastole, often after S3.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Large shunt or severe regurgitation 2 ↑ diastolic volume crosses normal AV valve 3 Turbulence → short rumble
Inspiration, expiration & maneuvers: Mitral flow ↑ expiration; tricuspid flow ↑ inspiration.
Diseases / conditions: Mitral: severe MR, VSD, PDA. Tricuspid: ASD, severe TR.
Where & how to listen: Apex (mitral) / LLSB (tricuspid), bell.
Key pearl: Implies a large shunt (Qp:Qs > 2:1).

Murmur: Patent ductus arteriosus PDA
Definition (whole): Continuous 'machinery' murmur from aorta → pulmonary artery through a persistent ductus.
Word-by-word: Patent = open · Ductus arteriosus = fetal vessel linking PA and aorta.
When / phase heard: Continuous (systole + diastole), peaks around S2.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Ductus fails to close after birth (normally ↑ O 2 , ↓ PGE 2 ) 2 Aortic > PA pressure all cycle → continuous L→R flow 3 LA/LV overload; wide pulse pressure 4 Eisenmenger → differential cyanosis (lower limbs)
Inspiration, expiration & maneuvers: Little change.
Diseases / conditions: Prematurity, congenital rubella, high altitude.
Where & how to listen: Left infraclavicular (1st–2nd LICS).
Key pearl: Indomethacin closes; PGE keeps open. 1

Murmur: Venous hum
Definition (whole): Benign continuous murmur from turbulent flow in the jugular veins.
Word-by-word: Venous = veins · Hum = soft continuous sound.
When / phase heard: Continuous, louder in diastole.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 High-velocity venous return from neck 2 Turbulence at jugular–subclavian/SVC junction
Inspiration, expiration & maneuvers: Louder sitting & inspiration; gone supine or with jugular pressure/head turn.
Diseases / conditions: Children, pregnancy, anemia, thyrotoxicosis. (Also mammary souffle: late pregnancy/lactation.)
Where & how to listen: Right supraclavicular.
Key pearl: Only innocent murmur that is continuous.

boxes.t: AV fistula / ruptured sinus of Valsalva
boxes.x:
Murmur: AV fistula / ruptured sinus of Valsalva
Definition (whole): Continuous murmurs from an abnormal high → low pressure connection.
Word-by-word: AV = artery–vein · Sinus of Valsalva = aortic root bulge above each cusp.
When / phase heard: Continuous.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 High-pressure vessel connects to low-pressure chamber/vein 2 Gradient persists in systole & diastole → continuous flow
Inspiration, expiration & maneuvers: Little change.
Diseases / conditions: Dialysis fistula, trauma, coronary AV fistula; sinus aneurysm rupture into RA/RV (sudden pain + HF).
Where & how to listen: Over the lesion; sinus: LSB.
Key pearl: Dialysis fistula: thrill/bruit = patent. Large fistula → high-output HF.

Murmur: Coarctation of aorta
Definition (whole): Systolic (± continuous) murmur from aortic narrowing, usually distal to left subclavian.
Word-by-word: Coarctation (L. coarctare) = to press together.
When / phase heard: Systolic (late); continuous from collaterals.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Narrowing → ↑ upper-body BP, ↓ lower-body BP 2 Turbulent flow at the site → systolic murmur 3 Intercostal collaterals dilate → continuous murmurs, rib notching
Inspiration, expiration & maneuvers: Little change.
Diseases / conditions: Turner syndrome, bicuspid aortic valve, berry aneurysm.
Where & how to listen: Left interscapular (back).
Key pearl: Radio-femoral delay; arm BP > leg; '3' sign on CXR.

Murmur: Pericardial friction rub (not a murmur)
Definition (whole): Scratchy, grating sound from inflamed pericardial layers rubbing.
Word-by-word: Friction rub = sound of two surfaces rubbing.
When / phase heard: Up to 3 components: atrial systole, ventricular systole, early diastole.
Pathophysiology (step by step): 1 Inflamed visceral & parietal pericardium lose smooth lubrication 2 Surfaces rub with every cardiac movement
Inspiration, expiration & maneuvers: Often ↑ inspiration; persists with breath-holding (pleural rub stops).
Diseases / conditions: Acute pericarditis: viral, uremic, post-MI/Dressler, autoimmune, TB, malignancy.
Where & how to listen: LLSB, sit up & lean forward, diaphragm.
Key pearl: Evanescent; may vanish as effusion grows.

cols.h: สรุปท้ายหน้า

boxes.x:
Grading (Levine)
Systolic 1–6: 1 faint · 2 soft · 3 loud, no thrill · 4 + thrill · 5 heard with edge of
stethoscope · 6 heard off chest. Diastolic graded 1–4.

Describe every murmur
Timing (systolic/diastolic/continuous) · shape · location · radiation · intensity
· pitch (bell/diaphragm) · quality (harsh, blowing, rumbling) · maneuvers.

Radiation cheat sheet
AS → carotids · MR → axilla · PS → left shoulder/back · Coarctation → back · AR
→ apex/LSB · HOCM & VSD → no carotid radiation.

Red flags → echo
Any diastolic or continuous murmur (except venous hum) · holosystolic · grade
≥3 or thrill · abnormal S2 · symptoms (syncope, chest pain, dyspnea) · cyanosis.

Mnemonic
Systolic = “MR. ASS” (MR, AS) · Diastolic = “MS. ARD” (MS, AR). Same logic on
the right: TR/PS systolic, TS/PR diastolic.
